topic: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
parentTitle: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
title: Epilepsy care and SUDEP
blurb: Support safe everyday epilepsy care for people with a learning disability: accurate seizure records, annual review, SUDEP risk reduction and valproate safety.
question: Jade, 26, has a learning disability and generalised tonic-clonic seizures, several of them at night. She sleeps alone and sometimes refuses her evening tablets. Her mother asks whether epilepsy can be fatal and what can be done. How should the nurse respond?

teach.body: Epilepsy is much more common in people with a learning disability than in the general population, and seizures may be harder to describe, recognise and treat. People may not be able to report auras, side effects or injuries. NICE NG217 asks for tailored information (longer appointments, easy read, involving family or an advocate) and at least annual review for adults with epilepsy and a learning disability. In plain English: good records, good communication and regular review keep people safe.

teach.h: SUDEP: say it, then reduce it
teach.body: Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) is a real risk. NICE NG217 asks professionals to discuss each person's individual risk of epilepsy-related death, including SUDEP, from diagnosis onwards with the person and, if appropriate, their family and carers, and to agree ways to reduce it. Modifiable risk factors include not taking medicines as prescribed, alcohol or drug misuse, tonic-clonic seizures, uncontrolled seizures, living alone and sleeping alone without supervision.

teach.caption: Alcohol and drug misuse and living alone are also on the NICE list.

teach.body: For people who have seizures during sleep and are assessed as at higher risk of epilepsy-related death, NICE says discuss introducing or increasing night-time supervision, for example a night monitor used by family or carers. Any monitoring must respect privacy and, if the person lacks capacity for the decision, be agreed in their best interests as the least restrictive option. Supporting people to take medicines as prescribed is one of the most powerful ways to reduce risk.

items.label: review for adults with epilepsy and LD (4.4.1)
lifetime SUDEP risk quoted by the NICE committee
valproate not started unless two specialists agree

teach.caption: The SUDEP figure is context from NICE's rationale; risk is highest with uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures.

teach.text: Do not explain every new seizure pattern as 'just their epilepsy'. A rise in seizures can be caused by missed doses (find out why: taste, tablet size, swallowing, side effects), constipation, illness, a new medicine that lowers the seizure threshold such as an antipsychotic, or, in Down syndrome, emerging Alzheimer's disease.

teach.body: The nurse answers honestly: epilepsy carries a risk of sudden death, and NICE expects that risk to be discussed and reduced. Jade's risks are uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures, missed evening doses and sleeping alone with night seizures. The nurse finds that Jade refuses the large tablet, so the prescriber switches to a liquid form. They discuss a night monitor with Jade using easy read information, Jade agrees, and her epilepsy care plan is updated and shared with her and her mother.

children.label: Do not start valproate
children.sub: Unless two specialists document no alternative

teach.caption: Valproate carries a high risk of birth defects and developmental disorders; women who can get pregnant need extra safeguards.

items: Record seizures in detail: before, during, duration, after, video with consent.
Adults with epilepsy and a learning disability need at least annual review (NG217 4.4.1).
Discuss SUDEP from diagnosis; reduce missed doses, uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures and unsupervised night seizures.
Discuss introducing or increasing night-time supervision, such as a monitor, for higher-risk nocturnal seizures (NG217 10.2.1).
Valproate is not started under 55 unless two specialists document no alternative.

summary: You can now keep accurate seizure records, explain and reduce SUDEP risk in line with NICE NG217, and support people to take their medicines safely. You can recognise when a change in seizures has another cause, and apply valproate safety rules.

A.q: Kieran, 32, has a severe learning disability and epilepsy. Staff record his seizures as 'had a funny turn'. What should the nurse put in place first?
options: A request to increase his anti-seizure medicine dose
A detailed seizure record with timing and recovery
A daily log of how many hours he sleeps each night
A plan to call 999 for every seizure staff witness
A.why: Accurate descriptions (before, during, duration, after, video with consent) let the specialist judge seizure type and control and adjust treatment.

whyNot.0: Changing doses without accurate information risks side effects without better control.
whyNot.2: Sleep can be a trigger, but it does not describe the seizures.
whyNot.3: His emergency plan should set when to call 999; not every seizure needs an ambulance.

A.q: How often does NICE NG217 say adults with epilepsy and a learning disability should have a monitoring review?
options: Every two years once stable
Every five years with the GP
When seizures are reported
At least once a year
A.why: NG217 4.4.1: arrange regular, at least annual, monitoring reviews for adults with epilepsy and a learning disability.

whyNot.0: Two-yearly is less often than NICE recommends for this group.
whyNot.1: Five-yearly review is far too infrequent.
whyNot.2: Waiting for reports misses side effects and silent problems.

A.q: Which of these is a modifiable risk factor for SUDEP listed in NICE NG217?
options: A family history of epilepsy in a parent
Female sex
Sleeping alone without supervision
Onset of epilepsy in childhood
A.why: NG217 10.1.2 lists non-adherence, alcohol and drug misuse, tonic-clonic seizures, uncontrolled seizures, living alone and sleeping alone without supervision.

whyNot.0: Family history cannot be changed and is not on the modifiable list.
whyNot.1: Sex is not a modifiable factor in NG217.
whyNot.3: Age of onset cannot be modified.

B.q: Oscar, 40, has a learning disability and frequent tonic-clonic seizures during sleep. He sleeps alone and his specialist rates his risk as high. What does NICE NG217 suggest?
options: Discuss night-time supervision or a monitor
Move him to a 24-hour nursing home
Give a sedative to stop the night seizures
Ask staff to check him once every four hours
B.why: NG217 10.2.1: discuss introducing or increasing night-time supervision, for example a night monitor, for people with seizures during sleep assessed as at higher risk.

whyNot.1: A care home move is far more restrictive than monitoring and not what NICE suggests.
whyNot.2: Sedation does not treat epilepsy and adds risk.
whyNot.3: Four-hourly checks could miss a seizure entirely; NICE suggests discussing supervision or a monitor.

B.q: Lily, 23, has a mild learning disability and focal seizures. Her neurologist is choosing a new anti-seizure medicine. Which medicine should not be started unless two specialists document there is no suitable alternative?
options: Levetiracetam
Lamotrigine
Carbamazepine (modified release)
Sodium valproate
B.why: MHRA measures reflected in NG217 (January 2025): valproate is not started in anyone under 55 unless two specialists independently document there is no other effective or tolerated treatment.

whyNot.0: Levetiracetam is not subject to this two-specialist rule.
whyNot.1: Lamotrigine is not subject to this rule.
whyNot.2: Carbamazepine is not subject to the valproate rule.

B.q: Freya, 29, has a learning disability and epilepsy and wants to start swimming. Her support worker thinks she should not be allowed. What is the best response?
options: Agree, because swimming is unsafe for anyone with seizures
Support a risk assessment so she can swim with safeguards
Allow it if she stops her medicine on swimming days
Suggest she uses a bath at home to swim-practise instead
B.why: People with epilepsy are supported to live full lives; NG217 lists safety issues and adapted activities for discussion. An individual risk assessment and plan (such as a trained companion) is proportionate.

whyNot.0: A blanket ban is not person-centred; risks are managed individually.
whyNot.2: Stopping medicine increases seizure risk, including SUDEP.
whyNot.3: Baths carry a drowning risk; NG217 suggests showers rather than baths.

C.q: Sean, 34, has a severe learning disability and epilepsy. Over a month his seizures have increased. Staff find tablets hidden in his room and he spits out his morning dose. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give his tablets covertly in food from tomorrow
Report the increase to his neurologist and ask for a higher dose
Find out why he refuses and review the form with the prescriber
Record the refusals and continue to offer the tablets
C.why: The increase is likely due to missed doses, so the reason for refusal (taste, tablet size, swallowing, side effects) must be found and the formulation reviewed. Supporting adherence is a NICE priority for reducing SUDEP risk (NG217 10.2.2).

whyNot.0: Covert medicines need a capacity assessment and an MDT best interests decision first.
whyNot.1: A dose rise does not help if he is not taking the medicine.
whyNot.3: Recording alone leaves him at rising risk of seizures and SUDEP.

C.q: Jade, 26, has a learning disability and night-time tonic-clonic seizures. Her mother asks, 'Could Jade die from her epilepsy?' What is the best response?
options: Explain there is a risk and discuss ways to reduce it
Reassure her that deaths happen only with severe epilepsy
Say this should wait until Jade's neurologist reviews her
Avoid the topic to prevent causing Jade and her mother worry
C.why: NG217 10.1.4: discuss individual risk of epilepsy-related death, including SUDEP, from diagnosis onwards with the person and family, and agree ways to reduce it.

whyNot.1: False reassurance is inaccurate; uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures raise SUDEP risk.
whyNot.2: NICE expects this discussion from diagnosis; any professional can begin it honestly.
whyNot.3: Avoiding the topic denies them information they need to reduce risk.

C.q: Abdul, 45, has a profound learning disability and epilepsy. His seizure frequency has doubled over two weeks. He has not opened his bowels for six days. No medicines have changed. What should the nurse consider first?
options: A sign of worsening epilepsy needing a higher dose
Constipation contributing to his increased seizures
A sign of a new psychiatric illness developing
A side effect of his long-term anti-seizure medicine
C.why: PHE guidance notes that people with epilepsy may have more seizures when constipated. Six days without a bowel movement is a likely, treatable cause that needs action.

whyNot.0: Increasing the dose before treating a clear trigger adds side effects without fixing the cause.
whyNot.2: Nothing in the scenario suggests mental illness.
whyNot.3: His medicines are unchanged; a new trigger is more likely.

reteach.title: Three questions for every person with epilepsy
reteach.question: If you remember only three things to check, what should they be?

blocks.body: Records: are seizures described in detail? Risk: has SUDEP been discussed and are the modifiable factors (missed doses, uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures, sleeping unsupervised) being reduced? Review: has an adult with a learning disability had a review in the past year?

blocks.text: More seizures is a symptom with a cause: missed doses, constipation, illness or a new medicine. Look before raising the dose.

explain.body: Describe what happened before, during and after; time it; note injuries and recovery; video with consent. This helps the specialist identify seizure type.

test.q: Which detail in a seizure record is most useful for deciding whether emergency medicine is needed next time?
options: The exact duration of the seizure
The name of the staff member present
The room where the seizure happened
What the person ate that morning
test.why: Duration determines whether a seizure is prolonged or status epilepticus (5 minutes or more) and when rescue medicine is due.

whyNot.1: Who was present does not guide treatment.
whyNot.2: Location may help with triggers but not with emergency decisions.
whyNot.3: Food may be a trigger clue but does not set emergency treatment.

explain.body: NG217 4.4.1: at least annual review for adults with epilepsy and a learning disability. 2.1.4: longer appointments, easy read, involve family or an advocate.

test.q: Which adjustment does NICE NG217 suggest for epilepsy appointments with people who have a learning disability?
options: Shorter appointments to reduce anxiety
Information in formats such as easy read
Seeing carers without the person present
Postal reviews in place of face-to-face meetings
test.why: NG217 2.1.4: give longer appointments and information in different formats such as easy read, and involve family or an advocate if the person wishes.

whyNot.0: NICE suggests longer appointments, not shorter.
whyNot.2: The person is included; carers are involved alongside them.
whyNot.3: Postal contact is not the adjustment NICE describes.

explain.body: Non-adherence, alcohol or drug misuse, tonic-clonic seizures, uncontrolled seizures, living alone, sleeping alone without supervision (NG217 10.1.2).

test.q: A man with uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures often forgets his evening tablets. Which action most directly reduces his SUDEP risk?
options: Moving his appointments to the morning
Reducing his fluid intake in the late evening hours
Supporting him to take medicines as prescribed
Asking him to stop playing weekly football
test.why: NG217 10.2.2: support people to take medicines as prescribed to reduce seizures; uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures raise SUDEP risk.

whyNot.0: Appointment times do not affect adherence to evening doses.
whyNot.1: Fluids are not a SUDEP factor.
whyNot.3: Exercise is not a listed SUDEP risk factor and has health benefits.

explain.body: Valproate is not started in anyone under 55 unless two specialists independently document no other suitable treatment (MHRA, reflected in NG217 January 2025).

test.q: A 30-year-old man with a learning disability has new generalised seizures. Can valproate be started?
options: Yes, as men are not affected by MHRA rules
Yes, if his parents agree in his best interests
No, valproate is banned for people with epilepsy
Yes, if two specialists document no alternative
test.why: MHRA rules: valproate is not started under 55 unless two specialists independently document there is no other effective or tolerated option. This applies to men and women.

whyNot.0: The under-55 rule applies to men too.
whyNot.1: Parental agreement does not replace the two-specialist requirement.
